Prime Minister Narendra Modi had in 2015 launched the Skill India Mission, which has an ambitious target of imparting skills to about 40.2 crore workers by 2022. """

- Hopeful

- Optimistic
- Pessimistic

The article mentions the launch of the Skill India Mission and the upcoming release of a new definition of skills that is aligned with international standards. 'Sorry but we can't let you do that,' said Al. 'So we decided to scrounge what we could, pool it and see what we ended up with.'

response:

Bats emit high-pitched sounds, called echolocation calls or pulses, from their larynx or nasal passages. These calls travel through the air and reflect off nearby objects, such as trees, insects, or prey. When the reflected echoes reach the bat's ears, they are processed by the brain to form an auditory image of the environment.

The frequency of these echolocation calls ranges from around 20 kHz to over 100 kHz, which is much higher than the range of human hearing (around 20 Hz to 20 kHz). This high frequency allows bats to produce narrow beams of sound, similar to a flashlight, that can penetrate through obstacles and illuminate the surroundings.

response:
A sweatshop is a type of factory or workplace characterized by poor working conditions, long hours, low wages, and exploitation of workers, especially in developing countries. These factories often produce goods for export to more affluent nations, such as clothing, electronics, and toys. Some common criticisms of the sweatshop labor model include:

1. Poor Working Conditions: Sweatshops often lack basic safety measures, proper ventilation, lighting, and sanitation facilities. Workers are exposed to hazardous materials, noise pollution, and dangerous machinery without adequate protection.

2. Long Hours: Employees in sweatshops may be required to work up to 16-hour shifts, seven days a week, with little or no overtime pay. This leaves little time for rest, leisure, or education.

3. Low Wages: Despite working long hours, sweatshop workers are paid meager wages that barely cover their living expenses. Many live in poverty and struggle to provide for their families.

4. Child Labor: Some sweatshops employ children as young as six years old, subjecting them to dangerous working conditions and denying them an education and childhood.

5. Lack of Job Security: Workers in sweatshops have little job security, as they can be fired at any time without notice or compensation. They also lack basic labor rights, such as the right to form unions or negotiate collective bargaining agreements.

These criticisms highlight the human cost of cheap labor and call into question the morality and sustainability of the global economy's reliance on sweatshops. While some argue that sweatshops offer employment opportunities in impoverished regions, others contend that they perpetuate poverty, exploitation, and social inequality. Ultimately, it is up to consumers, governments, and businesses to ensure that workers around the world are treated fairly and with dignity.

IKEA on Tuesday started selling its products on Alibaba's Chinese e-commerce platform Tmall, the first time the world's biggest furniture retailer has sold through a third party in its 77-year history.

The move is aimed at reaching more shoppers in a country where shoppers to a larger extent than elsewhere favour multi-brand online platforms.

IKEA said it saw its virtual store on Tmall - initially a six-month test across the east coast provinces of Jiangsu, Zhejiang and Anhui, and the city of Shanghai - as a complement to its own stores, online store and shoppable app.

"We see this as a good opportunity to become accessible for many more in China, especially in light of what the Chinese digital environment looks like," Tolga Oncu, head of retail at Ingka, which owns most IKEA stores worldwide, told Reuters.

"We are testing this to see 'how does this impact our brand, how does this impact our infrastructure, our own stores and e-commerce, do we reach new segments ... and of course also what will the result look like'," he said in an interview.

The trial marks another attempt to adapt to rapidly changing shopping patterns for the group, which until a decade ago almost solely relied on its giant out-of-town warehouse stores.

To become more accessible, IKEA has in recent years invested heavily in expanding online and in new sales channels. It is now rolling out a new shoppable app as well as inner-city store formats.

If the test proves successful, IKEA aims to roll the Tmall store out to more parts of China. But there are no plans currently to sell through third parties in other markets, said Jon Abrahamsson Ring, incoming CEO at brand owner Inter IKEA.

"In other markets there are other conditions. So we dont see this as a starting point for a full roll-out, or a full commitment to this type of channel," Abrahamsson Ring said.

IKEA sees China as a key growth market. The store on Tmall will offer around 3,800 of IKEA's around 9,500 products as well as services available in its own sales channels, such as delivery and assembly.

IKEA has 30 stores in China, around half of which have been closed since January due to the coronavirus outbreak that has locked down large parts of China, spurring a move to home delivery as people steer clear of shopping malls and as people in quarantine spend much more time at home.
